title: Pronomi Diretti
subtitle: Mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le — replacing a direct object to avoid repeating it.
objectives: Identify a direct object and choose the matching pronoun
Place direct object pronouns correctly before a conjugated verb
Make the past participle agree with lo/la/li/le in the passato prossimo

content.intro: Once you've mentioned something, Italian — like English — lets you replace it with a pronoun instead of repeating the noun. Direct object pronouns go before the verb, which takes some getting used to for English speakers.
content.explanation: A direct object answers "what?" or "whom?" with no preposition: in Leggo il libro, il libro is the direct object, replaceable by lo: Lo leggo. Unlike English ("I read it"), the pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, not after.

rules.heading: a) Position
rules.body: Before a conjugated verb: La conosco bene. Attached to an infinitive (dropping its final -e): Voglio conoscerla. (also correct: La voglio conoscere.)

rules.heading: b) Agreement in the passato prossimo
rules.body: With avere, lo/la/li/le force the past participle to agree, even though avere verbs otherwise never agree: Ho comprato la macchina. → L'ho comprata. (Lo/la elide to l' before a vowel.)

examples.it: Compro il pane. Lo compro ogni giorno.
examples.en: I buy bread. I buy it every day.

examples.it: Vedi Maria stasera? Sì, la vedo alle otto.
examples.en: Are you seeing Maria tonight? Yes, I'm seeing her at eight.

examples.it: Hai visto i miei occhiali? Non li trovo.
examples.en: Have you seen my glasses? I can't find them.

examples.it: Ho comprato le mele e le ho lavate.
examples.en: I bought the apples and washed them.

commonMistakes.why: The direct object pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, not after, unlike English.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ho comprato la e ho mangiato la. (for la mela)
commonMistakes.why: Lo/la elide to l' before a vowel (ho), and the participle must agree: comprata, not comprato.
The pronoun must precede the verb, and the participle agrees with li: visti.

items.explanation: La pizza is feminine singular → la.
I biglietti is masculine plural → li.

items.prompt: How do you say "I bought them" (le chiavi, feminine plural, passato prossimo)?
items.explanation: Le goes before ho, and the participle agrees: comprate.

items.prompt: Guardo la TV. → ___ guardo ogni sera.
items.explanation: La TV is feminine singular → la.

items.prompt: Vedo i miei amici. → ___ vedo spesso.
items.explanation: I miei amici is masculine plural → li.

items.prompt: "Le ho viste ieri" — le refers to...
items.explanation: Le is the feminine plural direct object pronoun.

items.statement: Direct object pronouns always go after the conjugated verb, as in English.
items.explanation: They go before the conjugated verb in Italian, unlike English.

summary: Direct object pronouns (mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le) replace a direct object and go before the conjugated verb.
They can attach to an infinitive instead, dropping its final -e.
With avere in the passato prossimo, lo/la/li/le force participle agreement — the one exception to "avere never agrees".
